title: Inquest to judge driver's intention: Cocaine-addled man was killed after fleeing police in stolen truck
article: Stuck on a hill with nowhere to go but towards a pursuing RCMP cruiser, a cocaine-fuelled Steven Hanaghan threw his truck in reverse and hit the gas pedal.

Whether he was attempting to go around an RCMP dog handler stopped on the narrow gravel road in Westsyde -- or directly at them -- was the focus of conflicting testimony at a coroner's inquest Monday.
Pathologist Dr. David Stefanelli told a five-person jury that when Hanaghan made that decision, he had enough cocaine and crack cocaine in his system to be intoxicated by the drugs.
"A person would be less in control of themselves and more likely to make bad decisions," he said.

Hanaghan, 45, was killed shortly after 5 a.m. on June 27, 2005 when Const. Tod Abram fired three shots into the stolen Chevrolet truck he was driving. Stefanelli confirmed Hanaghan died from a single gunshot wound.
The incident began earlier that morning when Hanaghan and his friend, Stephen Cikes, tried backing the truck through the front door of the Super Save gas station on Westsyde Road.
That effort was foiled by concrete posts placed in front of the door. The men drove north towards The Dunes golf course. A resident witnessed the attempted break-in and called police.
A police cruiser driven by Const. Ralph Overby caught up with Hanaghan and Cikes near The Dunes. Cikes told the jury that at that point Hanaghan asked him what he wanted to do.
"I told him he was driving and it was up to him," Cikes said.
This started a 13-kilometre pursuit. The vehicles raced along at speeds reaching 126 km/h until Hanaghan turned onto Noble Creek Road.
This is where Abram, a dog handler, joined the pursuit. He had just gone off duty when the call was dispatched, but he decided to help out.
Cikes said Hanaghan used a fork in the road to lose Overby. He turned right, then made a sudden turn "overland." Abram caught up with Hanaghan on the left fork and continued the chase.

The suspects' escape came to an end when Hanaghan was forced to switch gas tanks. The vehicle was chugging up a hill and lost momentum. Hanaghan was forced to stop. Abram said he got out of his SUV with his dog in case the pair decided to flee.
At this point Cikes's and Abram's testimony differ. Cikes said Hanaghan put the truck into reverse to swerve around the police vehicle. Instead, he hit it.
He said Abram was "between 25 and 30 feet away" when the vehicles collided. He said Abram opened fire as he walked towards the vehicle.
"I heard some shots and Steve got hit," he said.
Abram yelled for the men to get out of the vehicle. Cikes complied but said Hanaghan was shot.
"He (Abram) said 'you get out or I'll shoot you too,' " Cikes said.
Abram testified that he yelled repeatedly for Hanaghan to stop and get out of the vehicle. He told the jury he was unable to move as the vehicle reversed towards him.
"My feet felt like they were planted there," he said, indicating he feared for his life.
"The truck was coming very fast at me. I pulled my handgun and pointed it at the vehicle and continued to yell at them to stop."
He fired his shots by the time the vehicles collided.
Overby took Cikes into custody while Abram attempted to revive Hanaghan. Hanaghan bled to death within minutes of being shot.

Const. Gerard Poitras, an RCMP collision deconstructionist, said evidence at the scene showed the Chevy slid slightly to the right when it stopped on the road. There was not enough room for the vehicle to manoeuvre around the SUV.
Ballistic evidence suggests Abram was near the front of his SUV when he opened fire, Poitras said.
The inquest before Assistant Deputy Chief Coroner Jeff Dolan continues today.
